content: The documentation of the model should include a detailed explanation of the chosen parameter ranges and the justification for these values. While it is unlikely that the model will be replicated to validate the analytical results, the documentation must be sufficiently detailed to allow for such replication if needed. Any adaptations made to the model for specific applications should also be clearly documented. Ideally, the computer programming code used in the model should be made available. During the preparation of modeling results for use in a country application to the Global Fund, the structure of the model, along with its strengths and limitations, was extensively discussed with in-country stakeholders. Additionally, a smaller in-country modeling team tested the key assumptions and functionality of the model. This process of opening up the black box of the model led to critical questions that improved the model's structure, documentation, and calibration to country-specific data. A detailed description of alternative scenarios assessed in a particular application, including how these scenarios were developed, should be provided. Many applications include a comparison with a business-as-usual base case, and this should also be clearly described. Results from the modeled analysis should be accompanied by a non-technical explanation of uncertainties, limitations, the evidence sources supporting major assumptions, and the extent to which the model has been validated for the research question at hand. In cases where major policy decisions might be delayed until further studies are conducted, this should be explicitly stated. In situations where modeling results may be contentious, additional efforts should be made to engage all relevant stakeholders early in the modeling process. Broad review, input, and agreement on draft versions of policy scenarios and results should be sought. Information on the approach used to identify participants in the modeling process should also be reported. At the planning stage of a modeling exercise, any major conflicts of interest among parties involved should be identified, and a plan for managing these conflicts should be developed. External expert review of the modeling approach and results can be valuable. Such reviews, conducted either during the analysis phase or after the modeling is completed, can help donors or local decision-makers assess the strengths and limitations of the analysis and better understand the implications of the results for decision-making. Modeling activities should be organized to provide results at the time they are required for decision-making. While this principle ideally does not conflict with other principles, in practice, the need to produce results quickly can limit opportunities to test all aspects of a model and reduce the time available for stakeholders to review results, raise questions, and refine scenarios. At the start of a modeling project, the timeline for when evidence is needed to support decision-making should be identified, and a timeframe should be developed to meet this target, including sufficient time for review and revision of scenarios and assumptions. Modeling should be conducted with the full participation of local stakeholders at every stage of the process. This ensures that modeling assumptions and scenarios are more likely to be appropriate and that results are fully understood and considered by policymakers. However, country ownership is not guaranteed in situations where modeling is conducted by external technical experts or dictated by external funding agencies. In such cases, greater efforts may be needed to engage all relevant stakeholders fully. Coordination with existing initiatives for data collection and use in program planning can improve the quality of data available for modeling and reduce the likelihood of conflicting policy advice being provided to decision-makers. An initial task of a modeling project is to identify and engage relevant country stakeholders, including representatives from the National TB Program (NTP), non-governmental organizations (NGOs), patient advocacy groups, local subject-matter experts, and representatives of international funders and technical partners. The desire for in-country capacity-building should be assessed and addressed early in the project. This could involve enabling key partners in the NTP to critically examine model assumptions and results or building the capacity needed to operate the model without external technical assistance. Country input should be enabled at every stage of the modeling process, including determining whether key epidemiological and cost targets are satisfactorily reflected, making decisions on intervention scenarios, and reviewing modeling results before dissemination to a wider audience. Any new modeling application should be planned in light of existing efforts in research, evaluation, surveillance, and technical assistance designed to inform policy and planning. If modeling is to be undertaken by an external technical assistance provider, the choice of provider should depend on their ability to meet the needs of country decision-makers. This includes familiarity with the setting and questions of interest, the ability to produce results within the required timeframe, and providing sufficient opportunities for input and critical review of results. Modeling should involve an iterative process of engagement and should be reconsidered in light of new evidence. Given the complexity of modeling and decision-making, an iterative process is likely needed to identify candidate policies or interventions and the evidence to describe them. The modeling approach should allow for iteration between model adaptation and evaluation of results. Once a modeling exercise is complete, the results should remain open to criticism and revision as new evidence becomes available, and a clear path forward for improving the process should be identified. In a given modeling application, there should be multiple opportunities for key stakeholders to review model scenarios and results. Explanations should be sufficient for stakeholders to understand major analytic decisions and assumptions, and analyses should be revised in light of feedback. Modeling results should be accompanied by an explanation of the sensitivity of results to new evidence, research that would be useful to validate the results, and findings that should trigger a revision of the analysis. As new policies are introduced, early programmatic data can be used to check assumptions made during modeling. If assumptions are incorrect, the validity of longer-term projections should be reconsidered. If necessary, model projections may be updated based on actual implementation data. Modeling groups have evaluated past projections and results in light of new burden estimates or data, such as prevalence surveys or inventory studies. For example, as part of preparations for a Global Fund application, one modeling group reviewed previous projections in the context of new prevalence survey data. The modeling process involves defining the decision or problem, identifying decision-makers, and defining the policies to be compared and the outcomes of interest. At this early stage, it is important to determine whether mathematical modeling is the appropriate approach to answer the policy question. If modeling is deemed appropriate, the next step is to identify important stakeholders and relevant experts and form the project team that will collaborate on the modeling exercise. Once these have been determined, the next step is to define the timeframe for the work and how it fits into the policy and planning cycle. The choice of model used should be based on its suitability for the required needs, including whether it includes relevant risk groups, stratifications, interventions, or epidemiological characteristics. The suitability of a model structure will also depend on the time and labor requirements to undertake the analysis and the ability to provide training and capacity development if requested. In some situations, only one model may be available for a particular application, but this does not remove the need to critically evaluate its suitability for the country context and policy questions being asked. Once the first stage has been firmly established, the next step is to identify the required resources for the work, including the expertise of in-country decision-makers, epidemiologists, and costing experts, as well as technical assistance. The availability of sufficient funding for the work, whether from in-country or external donors, should also be identified. A plan for developing institutional or in-country capacity should be established to ensure the work can be continued in the future. At this point, the modeling team, typically including an external modeling group, should be formally formed. Once the team has been formed, the model can begin to be used to generate results, which should then be examined and interpreted by the relevant experts. The subsequent stage, reporting of the model results, highlights the need to describe key assumptions made in the modeling, include the sources of various data used, describe the model results, and identify limitations to the modeling approach. Finally, follow-up is needed after the reporting of model results. This includes follow-up related to translating results into action, ensuring the sustainability of the process, and testing the model as new data becomes available.
